But what you seem to me, having suffered at the hands of others, reasonably to suspect of all—seeing always some one of the consuls who summons you to the wars promising to obtain from the senate whatever you need, yet bringing none of the agreements to fulfilment—that you would not justly suspect this of me too, I would prove especially by these two things: that the senate would not have used me for this service, when there were others more suited, the one thought most devoted to the people; and that it would not have adorned me with autocratic power, by which I shall be able to ratify what seems best to me even without it.

41.1. "For surely you do not suppose that I, knowing the deceit, have purposed to deceive you along with it and to do mischief together with it. For if these things enter your minds about me, as the most knavish of all men—use me as you wish; but free your souls of this suspicion by trusting me, and transfer your anger from your friends to the enemy, who come to take your city from you and to make you slaves instead of free, and who, hastening to inflict all the things accounted dreadful among men, are reported to be not far from our territory.

41.2. "Eagerly, then, clear yourselves of these slanders, and show them that even in faction the power of the Romans is stronger than another's at concord; for either they will not withstand you advancing with one accord, or they will pay penalties worthy of their daring. For consider that it is Volscians and Sabines, whom you have often conquered in battle, who bring war upon you, having now gained neither greater bodies nor braver souls than before, but, despising you as men at enmity with one another. And when you have punished the enemy, I pledge you that the senate will, worthily of the valour you display in the war, arbitrate both the rivalries over debts and whatever else you ask of it that is moderate.

41.3. "Meanwhile let every property, every person, every right of a Roman citizen be free from seizure for debt and every other contract. And to those who fight eagerly, the fairest crown shall be this city that bore you standing upright; fair too the praise of their fellows; and the adornment from us shall be enough to set right a household with money and make a family illustrious with honours. And I think fit that my own readiness for dangers be an example to you; for I will fight in the forefront as the mightiest of you."

42.1. When he had said this, the whole people, hearing it gladly, as men no longer to be deceived, promised to share in the war; and ten military legions were formed, each of four thousand men. Of these each of the consuls took three, with as many cavalry as were apportioned to each; the four others and the rest of the cavalry the dictator took. And at once, having made ready, they marched out with speed—Titus Veturius against the Aequians, Aulus Verginius against the Volscians, and the dictator Valerius himself against the Sabines; while Titus Larcius guarded the city with the elders and a small force of men in their prime.

42.2. The Volscian war reached a swift decision. For thinking they greatly surpassed in numbers and remembering their former misfortunes, having become fighters quicker rather than wiser by necessity, they rushed first upon the Romans, when they were seen encamped within view. A fierce battle ensuing, after doing many noble deeds but suffering more dreadful ones, they were turned to flight; their camp was taken, and a notable city was reduced by siege—Velitrae

42.3. was its name. In like manner the spirit of the Sabines too was humbled in a very short time, by a single pitched battle in which both wished to prevail. Then the country was plundered and certain small towns were taken, from which the soldiers got much both of persons and goods. The Aequians, suspecting their own weakness when they learned that their allies' affairs were at an end, sat down in strong places and did not come forth to battle, making their retreats, where they could, secretly through mountains or thickets; and they protracted the war for a while, dragging it out. Yet they could not bring their army off unharmed, since the Romans attacked them boldly in precipitous places and took their camp by storm. Then there was a flight of them from the Latin land and surrenders of the cities they happened to have seized at the first assault, and there were captures of citadels not abandoned out of obstinacy.

43.1. Valerius, the war having gone according to his mind, after leading home the customary triumph for the victory, dismissed the people from the campaign—though the senate did not yet think it the time, lest the poor demand the promises; and into the conquered land, which they had taken from the Volscians, he sent colonists, chosen from among the poor, who were both to garrison the enemy country and to leave behind less of the factious element in the city.

43.2. Having arranged these things, he asked the senate to confirm to him the promises, since it had received the eagerness of the multitude in the contests. But when it gave no heed to him, but—as before it had opposed him—the young and violent, gathering themselves and prevailing in number over the others, then too acted against him and made much outcry, declaring his house a fawner upon the people and the author of wicked laws, and blaming on that policy of the courts, in which the men most gloried in the assembly, the destruction of all the power of the patricians, Valerius, indignant at much and reproaching the people as suffering injustice in being slandered by them, and bewailing the fortune about to seize them for resolving such things, and, as is likely in such an evil, partly from passion and partly from understanding more than the many, prophesying, went away from the senate-house; and summoning the people to an assembly, he said:

43.3. "Owing you much gratitude, citizens, both for the zeal you showed me in joining willingly in the war and still more for the valour you displayed in the contests, I was making great effort to requite you both in other ways and by not falsifying the promises which I made to you on behalf of the senate, and by at last establishing your strife in concord, becoming counsellor and arbiter to both. But I am prevented from doing this by those who choose not the best things for the commonwealth, but what is for the moment pleasing to themselves, who, prevailing in number over the others and in the strength which youth furnishes them rather than the affairs, are emboldened.

43.4. "But I am old, as you see, and have others like me for allies, whose strength, lying in judgment, is unable to follow it up in deed; and our seeming care for the commonwealth has turned into what appears a private hatred toward each party. For by the senate I am blamed as courting your multitude, and to you I am slandered as showing my goodwill rather to it.

44.1. "If, then, the people, having been well treated, had failed of the promises made through me to the senate, I should have had this defence: that you broke faith, and there was no knavery in me; but since the things agreed by the senate have not been fulfilled to you, my speech now becomes necessary to the people: that you have not suffered with my consent, but that we both alike have been deceived and overreached—and I more than you, who am not only wronged in what I have been deceived in common with all, but also in the things I have heard ill of privately—as that I gave the spoils taken from the enemy to your poor without the common consent of the council, wishing to win private favour, and that I think fit to confiscate the property of citizens, though it forbade me and bade me not transgress the law, and that I dismissed the army against the will of the senators, when I ought to have kept you amid the bivouacs and wanderings

44.2. in the enemy's country. I have also been reproached with the sending of the colonists to the Volscians, because I bestowed much good land not on the patricians nor the knights, but distributed it among your poor; and—what gave me the most indignation—because more than four hundred men from the people were enrolled among the knights at the levy, having grown wealthy.

44.3. "If, then, these things had befallen me while my body was in its prime, I should have made clear in deed to my enemies what manner of man they insulted; but since I am over seventy years of age and no longer able to defend myself, and I see that your strife would not even now be ended by me, I lay down my office and give my body to whoever wishes, if any think they have been deceived by me, to use as they judge just."

45.1. Having said this, he drew the whole commons to sympathy, and they escorted him as he departed from the Forum; but the senate he made still harsher toward himself. Straightway after this these things happened: the poor, no longer secretly nor by night as before, but now openly assembling, deliberated about a secession from the patricians; and the senate, purposing to prevent it, ordered the consuls not yet to disband the armies. For each was still master of three legions, the men being held by the military oaths and no one thinking fit to leave the standards—so great was the fear of the oaths in each man. A pretext for the campaign was contrived, that the Aequians and Sabines had joined together for the war against the Romans.

45.2. When the consuls had advanced outside the city with their forces and pitched their camps not far from one another, the soldiers, gathering all into one, being masters of arms and standards, at the instigation of one Sicinius Bellutus, seceded from the consuls, seizing the standards—for these the Romans hold most precious on campaign and consider sacred, like the shrines of the gods—and appointing other centurions and Sicinius commander over all, they seized a hill near the river Anio, not far from Rome, which from this is now called the Sacred Mount.

45.3. When the consuls and centurions recalled them with entreaty and lamentation and many promises, Sicinius answered: "With what intent, patricians, do you now recall those whom you drove from their country and made slaves instead of free? With what pledge will you confirm the promises to us which you are proved to have often falsified? But since you think fit to hold the city alone, depart, troubled no more by the poor and humble; for us, any land in which we have our freedom, whatever it be, will suffice to be reckoned our country."

46.1. When this was reported to those in the city, there was much tumult and lamentation and running through the streets, the people preparing to leave the city and the patricians thinking fit to turn them back and apply force to the unwilling; and there was an outcry about the gates and much wailing, and hostile words against one another, and the deeds of enemies, no one any longer distinguishing age or comradeship or worth of valour.

46.2. When those appointed by the senate to guard the exits—for they were few and no longer able to hold out—being forced out by the people, abandoned their watch, then at once the commons poured out in numbers, and the calamity was like the capture of a city, lamentation arising among those who remained and mutual reproaches as they saw the city being emptied. After this there were many councils and accusations of the authors of the secession. At the same time the enemy nations attacked them, plundering the land up to the city. The seceders, however, taking the necessary provisions from the nearby fields but doing no other harm to the country, remained in the open, and received those who came to them from the city and the surrounding forts, who were now becoming numerous.

46.3. For not only those who wished to escape debts and judgments and the expected necessities flocked to them, but also of the others, all whose life was idle or slack, or unable to supply their desires, or who were emulators of wicked practices, or envious of others' good fortune, or, through some other misfortune or cause, ill-disposed toward the established polity.

47.1. Upon the patricians at the moment fell much confusion and dismay, and fear lest the seceders, along with the foreign enemies, would presently come against the city. Then, as at a single command, snatching up their arms, each with his own clients, some went to the roads by which they thought the enemy would come, others marched out to the forts to guard the strongholds, and others encamped in the plains before the city; while those who through old age were unable to do any of these things were posted on the walls.

47.2. But when they learned that the seceders neither joined the enemy nor ravaged the country nor did any harm worth mentioning, they ceased from their fear; and changing their minds, they considered on what terms they should be reconciled with them. And speeches of all kinds, and most differing from one another, were made by the leaders of the council; but the most moderate and most fitting to the present fortunes were those which their eldest spoke, teaching that the people had made the secession from them through no wickedness, but partly forced by their unavoidable misfortunes, partly deceived by their counsellors, judging their interests by anger rather than reason, as is wont to happen among an ignorant multitude; and that most of them were conscious of having taken bad counsel and were seeking specious pretexts to undo their errors; for their very deeds were those of men already repentant, and, if they got good hope for the future, the senate having voted them impunity and made a seemly reconciliation, they would gladly accept their own.

47.3. And those who gave this advice thought fit that the better men should not prove worse in anger than the worse, nor put off the reconciliation to that time when either the senseless would be forced to come to their senses, or the lesser evil would be cured by the greater—when their freedom would be taken away by themselves through the surrender of arms and the giving up of their persons; for this was near to impossible. Rather, by using moderation, the patricians should become the authors of expedient counsels and go first to the reconciliation, considering that to rule and govern belonged to the patricians,

47.4. but of friendship and peace ... to the good. And they declared that the dignity of the senate would be lessened not most in that wherein, bearing their unavoidable misfortunes nobly, they would govern in safety, but in that wherein, dealing ill-temperedly with their fortunes, they would overthrow the commonwealth. It was a work of folly, they said, to disregard safety while reaching for what was seemly; for it was desirable to attain both, but if one were debarred from either, the saving things must be reckoned more necessary than the more seemly. The conclusion of those who gave this advice was to send envoys to treat with the seceders about friendship, on the ground that they had committed no irreparable wrong.

48.1. These things seemed good to the senate; and after this, having chosen the most suitable men, it sent them to those in the camp, charging them to learn from them what they wanted and on what just terms they thought fit to return to the city; for if any of their demands were moderate and possible, the senate would not oppose them. For the present, then, if they laid down their arms and came down to the city, impunity for their offences would be theirs, and amnesty for the time to come; and if they took the best counsels for the commonwealth and risked themselves eagerly for their country, fair and

48.2. profitable returns. The envoys, having received these instructions, delivered them to those in the camp and discoursed accordingly. But the seceders did not accept the proposals; rather, with disdain and harshness and much irony they reproached the patricians for pretending not to know what the people wanted and on account of what necessities they had seceded from them, while granting them impunity from suffering any penalty for the secession, as though they were still masters—when they themselves needed the citizens' help, men who before long would have to face the foreign wars which would come against them in full force, against whom they could not even lift a hand, men who did not reckon their own safety their own good, but the good fortune of those who would fight alongside them. Finally they added this argument, that the patricians, now learning better the straits that gripped the city, would know against what kind of adversaries the contest would be for them; and they uttered many harsh threats.

48.3. The envoys, making no further reply to this, departed and reported to the patricians the answer of the seceders. The city, when it received these answers, fell into far greater confusion and fear than before; and the senate was able to find neither a remedy nor a delay, but, hearing for many days the abuse and accusations which its leaders made against one another, was dissolved. Nor was the body of the commons, however much still remained from goodwill toward the patricians or compelled by longing for their country, of the same mind, but a great part of it too, openly and secretly, was draining away, and nothing of what remained seemed secure. These things having happened, the consuls—for the time still left them of their office was short—appointed a day for the elections.

49.1. The people, when the time came in which the magistracies had to be ratified by an assembly gathered in the plain, since no one either sought the consulship or, when it was offered, would accept it, themselves appointed consuls from among those who had already held this office, men acceptable both to the people and to the aristocracy—Postumus Cominius and Spurius Cassius, by whom the Sabines had been defeated and made to renounce their leadership—in the seventy-second Olympiad, in which Tisicrates of Croton won the foot-race, Diognetus being archon at Athens.

49.2. These, taking up office on the Kalends of September, sooner than had been the custom of their predecessors, before transacting anything else convened the senate to discuss the return of the commoners, and asked to declare his opinion first a man who was then in the prime of his age and thought to surpass the others in understanding, and most of all praised for the choice of his policies—because he was of the middle order, neither magnifying the arrogance of the aristocrats nor permitting the people to do whatever they wished—Agrippa Menenius; who urged the senate to the reconciliation, speaking thus:

49.3. "If, senators, it had happened that all present held the same opinion, and no one was likely to be an obstacle to the reconciliation with the people, but it lay before us only to consider on what terms—whether just or not—we should be reconciled with them, I would have shown you in few words what I think.

49.4. "But since some think this very point still needs deliberation—whether it is better for us to come to terms with the seceders or to make war—I do not think it easy for me by a short statement to advise what should be done, but I must by a longer speech teach those of you who are ill-disposed toward the reconciliation that they urge the contrary of what is good; or, if they mean to frighten you, that they reckless of the greatest and most incurable evils stand in dread of the slightest of difficult things, which admit of easy remedy. And they have come to this through nothing else than that they judge their interest not by reason but by passion and madness.

49.5. "For how could those be said to foresee with their minds anything useful or possible, who suppose that so great a city, now mistress of so many affairs and become an object of envy and grievance to its neighbours, could either, without the commons, easily hold and preserve the nations under it, or could bring in another people in place of the worse, a better one, which would fight for its empire on its behalf and govern with it in much tranquillity, showing itself moderate both in peace and in war? For they could say nothing else, trusting in which they would think fit to bid you not accept the reconciliation.

50.1. "How full of simplicity each of these alternatives is, I would beg you to consider from the very facts, reflecting that, when the humbler sort have fallen into strife with you on account of those who used their misfortunes neither in a civic nor moderate spirit, and have withdrawn from the city, but do and intend you no further harm, but only consider how they may be reconciled without disgrace—many of those ill-disposed toward you, gladly accepting what fortune brought, have been roused in spirit, and think this longed-for opportunity is at hand, in which they

50.2. will overthrow your empire. The Aequians and Volscians, the Sabines and the nation of the Hernicans, besides having made no truce in their war against us, and chafing at their recent evils, are plundering our fields. And of Campania and Tyrrhenia, all that remains doubtfully detached from us—some openly revolts, some secretly prepares to. It seems too that the Latin kinship no longer remains securely friendly to us when put to the test, but a great part of it is reported to be sick with a longing—which all crave—for change;

50.3. and we, who once encamped against others, now sit hemmed within our walls, having left our land unsown and seeing our steadings plundered, our booty driven off and our servants deserting, with no remedy for our ills. And, suffering these things, do we still hope that the commons will be reconciled with us, knowing that it lies in our power to end the strife by a single decree?

51.1. "With our affairs in the field so ill, the dangers within the walls are no less terrible. For we have not for a long while prepared our allied forces as men about to be besieged, nor are we ourselves sufficient in number against so many enemy nations; and of the small and unworthy garrison, the greater part is of the commons—labourers, clients, and artisans, not at all sure guardians of a shaken aristocracy. And the continual desertions of these to the seceders that now occur

51.2. have made the whole suspect. Above all these, the gathering of provisions, being impossible while the land is held by the enemy, already threatens famine, and when we come into straits will threaten still more; and besides these, there is the war that lets us be at no time secure in mind. But all the terrors are surpassed by the women of the seceders and their infant children and their aged parents, who in pitiable garments and mourning attire wander to ruin through the Forum and the streets, weeping, supplicating, clasping each man's right hand and knees, bewailing the desolation that holds them and will hold them still more—a dreadful and unendurable sight.

51.3. "There is no one so savage in disposition that he is not overturned in soul at seeing these things, and feels something at the fortunes of men. So that, if we mean to be irreconcilable toward the commons, we must rid ourselves of these persons too—the one sort as useless for a siege, the others as not likely to remain firmly friendly. But if these too are driven out, what force will be left to guard the city? Or in what aid shall we trust to dare endure the dangers? Our own refuge and only sure hope, the flower of the patricians, is small, as you see, and not worth being proud of. Why, then, do those who advise enduring the war babble and deceive us, rather than openly advise surrendering the city now to the enemy without blood and without toil?

52.1. "But perhaps I am deluded in saying these things and think fit to fear what is not terrible; and the city now risks nothing but a change, no hard thing, and we could with much ease receive into it a labouring and client multitude from every nation and place. For this is what many of those who oppose the commons keep harping on—and, by Jupiter, not the basest of them.

52.2. "For some have come to such simplicity as to propose not saving counsels but impossible prayers; whom I would gladly ask, what surplus of time will be given us, engaged in such affairs, with the enemy so near the city? What pardon will there be for the delay and tarrying of the allies who are to come, in dangers that neither tarry nor delay? What man or god will furnish us safety and gather at leisure from every place and convey hither the aid? And further, who will those be who leave their own countries and migrate to us? Will it be those who have homes and hearths and livelihoods and the honour they enjoy among their fellow citizens through ancestral distinction or the fame of their own valour? And who would endure to leave behind his own goods to share scantily in others' evils? For they will not come hither to share in peace and luxury, but in dangers and war, of which the outcome is uncertain

52.3. whether it will be brought to a good issue. Or shall we bring in a multitude that is plebeian and homeless, such as was that which was driven from here—clearly through debts and judgments and like misfortunes—glad to settle wherever it may chance? Such a one, even if it should be otherwise good and moderate (that we may grant it this too), would on this very account—that it would be neither native nor of the same way of life, nor acquainted with the customs and laws and breeding among us—be far and altogether worse than the one we have.

53.1. "For the native man has here as hostages his children and wives and parents and many other persons of his own kin, and—by Jupiter—the longing for the very soil that reared him, which is necessary to all and not to be removed; but this summoned and intrusive multitude, if it became our fellow-dweller, having none of these things here, for what good would it think fit to risk itself, unless someone should promise to give it portions of land and a share of the city, however great, taking it from the present owners—a thing we do not think fit to share even with our citizens who have often fought for it? And perhaps it would not even be content with these alone if given, but would think fit to share equally with the patricians in honours and offices and the other goods.

53.2. "Therefore, if we shall not grant each of their demands, shall we have as enemies those who fail of them? But if we should concede, our country will be gone and our polity overthrown by ourselves. And I do not add here that in the present we need bodies fit for war, not farmers or labourers or merchants or those occupied in mechanical crafts, who would at the same time have to learn warfare and give proof of it; and hard is the trial of those unaccustomed; and necessarily such would be the rabble migrating from every nation.

53.3. "For I see no military alliance established for us, nor, should one appear unexpectedly, would I advise you to receive it readily within the walls, knowing many other cities enslaved by the armies brought in for their guard.

54.1. "Reflecting, then, on these things and on whatever else has been said by us before, and recalling moreover, in answer to those who summon us to the reconciliation, that not among us alone or first has poverty striven against wealth and lowliness against eminence, but in nearly all cities, both small and great, the lesser is for the most part set against the greater as an enemy—in which the leaders of the commonwealth, by using moderation, have saved their countries, but by using arrogance have, along with the other goods, destroyed themselves as well;

54.2. and that everything compounded of many parts is by nature liable to sicken in some one of its members; and besides these, that one must neither always cut off the ailing part of the human body—for the appearance of what is left would be ugly and its nature not long-enduring—nor expel the diseased portion of a civic fellowship; for the whole would not be long in perishing through its own parts in time; and considering how great is the power of necessity, to which alone even the gods yield, do not chafe against your fortunes, nor fill yourselves with arrogance and folly as if all would be according to our prayer, but bend and yield, using as examples of good counsel not foreign deeds, but our own.

55.1. "For both a single man and a whole city ought to take pride in the noblest of their own deeds, and to see that the rest will be in keeping with these. You, then, having already taken into your power many enemies by whom you had been most grievously wronged, were willing neither to destroy them nor to cast them from their own, but gave them back their houses and lands, allowed them to dwell in the countries they sprang from, and to some of them you have even granted to be of equal vote and your fellow citizens.

55.2. "And I have a deed of yours still more wonderful than this to tell: that even of your own citizens, many who had greatly wronged you, you released from punishment, casting your anger on the authors alone—among whom were those who colonised Antemnae and Crustumerium and Medullia and Fidenae, and many others. For why need I now enumerate all whom you, when conquered by siege, admonished with moderation and in civic fashion? And in no way did either danger or blame on this account befall the city; rather, your fairness is praised, and nothing of your safety has been diminished.

55.3. "Then will you who spare your enemies make war on your friends, and you who let go unpunished those who came into your power will punish those who helped you win your empire? And, while offering your own city as a safe refuge to all who need it, will you endure to drive from it the native-born, with whom you were reared and educated and shared many evils and goods in peace and in war? No—not if you wish to do what is just and befitting your own customs, and to judge the expedient without anger.

56.1. "But that the strife must be ended, one might say, we have recognised no less than you, and have shown much zeal; only try to say how we may end it. For you see how great is the arrogance about the people, who neither send to us about a settlement, though they are in the wrong, nor give to those sent by us civic and humane answers, but are haughty and threaten, and it is not easy to conjecture what they want. To these things what I advise be done

56.2. now, hear from me. I think the people are neither irreconcilable toward us nor will do any of the things they threaten, judging that their deeds are not like their words, but I think they are far more eager than we for a settlement. For we both dwell in our most honoured country and have our livelihoods and houses and families and all things of most worth in our own power; but they are without city and without hearth, deprived of the persons most necessary to them, and have no easy supply for their daily living.

56.3. "For what reason, then, if anyone should ask me, does the people not accept our proposals, though itself suffering ill, and yet send no embassy to us?—Because, by Jupiter, I would say, up to now it hears words from the senate, but sees no deed coming from them either humane or moderate, and thinks it has often been deceived by us, who always promise to take some forethought for it, but take none. And it does not endure to send an embassy, both fearing those here accustomed to accuse it, and dreading lest it fail of any of its demands.

56.4. "Perhaps too there may be in it some passion of foolish pride; and that is no marvel, since even among ourselves there are some in whom is this quarrelsomeness and contentiousness, who think fit, both privately and publicly, not to be worsted by their adversary, but ever seek by every means to prevail, and not first to grant any favour until they get the one to be benefited into their power. Reflecting, then, on these things, I think an embassy should be sent to the commoners from those most trusted by them;

56.5. "and I advise that the men to be sent be invested with full powers to settle the strife on whatever terms they themselves think just, referring nothing further to the senate; for they will know this. And those who now seem arrogant and harsh, when they learn that you truly are zealous for concord, will come down to more equitable terms, demanding nothing either shameful or impossible. For everything that is provoked, especially if it be humble, is wont to grow savage toward those who scorn it, but to be tamed toward those who court it."

57.1. When Menenius had said this, a great murmur fell upon the senate, and they talked among themselves in groups—those well disposed toward the commoners urging one another to bring all zeal that they might lead the people back to their country, since they had now gained as leader of that opinion the most distinguished of the aristocratic men; while the aristocrats, wishing above all that the polity should not be moved from the ancestral order, were at a loss what to do with the present circumstances, not thinking fit to change their purposes, yet unable to remain by their resolutions; and the uncommitted, who took the side of neither faction, wished to keep the peace and to consider how they should not be besieged.

57.2. When silence fell, the elder of the consuls, having praised Menenius for his nobility and thought fit that the rest should prove guardians like him, speaking what they thought with frankness and doing without hesitation what was resolved, called next, in the same manner, by name, asking him to declare his opinion, Manius Valerius, brother of him who had helped free the city from the kings, a man more devoted to the people than any of the aristocrats whatsoever.

58.1. He, rising, first reminded the senate of his own policies, and that, though he had often foretold the evils that would befall, they had treated his words with neglect; then he thought fit that those opposed to the reconciliation should not now seek moderate things, but, since they had not let the strife be removed when the city's differences were still small, at least now consider how it might quickly cease and not, advancing further, escape notice and become perhaps incurable, or, if not, hard to cure and the cause of many evils to them. And he declared that the demand of the commoners would no longer be the same as before, nor did he conjecture that the people would come to terms asking only release from debts, but would perhaps need some safeguard by which it might continue secure for the future;

58.2. for, since the office of dictator had come in, the law guarding their freedom had been abolished—the law which neither allowed the consuls to put to death any citizen untried, nor that the commoners worsted in trial by the patricians should be handed over to those who had condemned them, but gave to those who wished the right to transfer the judgments from the patricians to the people, and that whatever the people decided should be valid. And almost all the rest of the power of the commoners, of which in former times they had been masters, had been taken away—seeing that not even the triumph from the wars could be obtained from the senate for a man more deserving of this honour than any other, Publius Servilius

58.3. Priscus. At these things, suffering naturally, the many were dispirited and had wretched hopes for their safety, since neither consul nor dictator who wished to care for them had been able to, but one of them had even reaped insult and dishonour for his zeal and forethought on behalf of the many. And these things, he said, had been wrought by a conspiracy not of the most gracious of the patricians, but of certain insolent and grasping men, terribly eager for unjust gain, who, having enslaved many citizens for a great difference and at high interest, and applying to them cruel and arrogant compulsions, made the whole commons estranged from the aristocracy; and having formed a faction and proclaimed as its leader Appius Claudius, a man hating the people and oligarchic, through him confound all the city's affairs. And unless the sound part of the senate stood in their way, the city was in danger of some enslavement and overthrow. At the end he declared that he agreed to use the opinion of Menenius, and thought fit to send the embassy quickly; and that the men, when they came, should try to settle the strife as they wished, but, if no one should grant them what they wanted, should accept what was given.

59.1. After him rose, when called, Appius Claudius, the leader of the faction opposed to the people, a man thinking much of himself, and that not without just cause; for his daily private life was temperate and grave, and the choice of his policies was noble and preserved the dignity of the aristocracy. He, taking occasion from the harangue of Valerius, used such words as these:

59.2. "Valerius would have been less to blame, had he declared only his own opinion and not accused those who held the contrary; for he might have heard none of the evils that belong to him. But since it did not suffice him to advise such things as will make us slaves to none but the basest of the citizens, but he both laid hold of those who opposed him and made hostile mention of me, I see much necessity that I too should speak on these matters, and first clear myself of the slanders against me. For he has reproached me with a practice neither civic nor seemly—that I have chosen to make money from every source, and have deprived many of the poor of their freedom, and that the secession of the people has come about not least on my account—none of which it is easy for you to learn is either true or sound.

59.3. "Come, then, say, O Valerius, who are those whom I enslaved for debt? Whom of the citizens did I hold, or do I now hold, in bonds? Which of the seceders is deprived of his country through my cruelty or love of money? But you could not say. For so far am I from having enslaved any citizen for debt, that, having given out my own to very many, I made none of those who defrauded me liable to seizure or dishonour, but all are free, and all owe me thanks and are counted among my friends and clients in matters most necessary. And I say this not to accuse those who have not done the like with me, nor do I think those wrong who did some act allowed by law; but I am clearing myself of the slanders against me.

60.1. "As for what he reproached me with as to harshness and the patronage of wicked men, calling me a hater of the people and oligarchic because I cling to the aristocracy—these are common accusations against all of you, as many as think fit, being the better, not to be ruled by the worse, nor to have the polity you inherited from your forefathers taken away by the basest of all polities among men, democracy.

60.2. "For let not this man give the name of oligarchy to the leadership of the best, as though the thing, slandered by the name, would thereby be obliterated; but we might far more justly and truly bring the reproach of demagogy and a longing for tyrannic deeds. For it is unclear to no one that every tyrant springs from a fawner upon the people, and that the road is swift for those who wish to enslave cities which leads through the basest citizens to despotic power; whom this man has continued to court and

60.3. does not even now cease. For know well that the base and humble would not have dared to commit so great offences, had they not been roused by this grave and patriotic man, on the ground that the deed would be without danger to them, and that, besides paying no penalty, they would have a better lot than before. And you would learn that I speak the truth, recalling that, while frightening you about war and declaring the reconciliation necessary, he at the same time said that the poor would not be content to be released from their debts, but would need some safeguard too, and would no longer endure to be ruled by you as before; and at the end he thought fit that you should be content with the present and concede whatever the people should think right to take on its return, not distinguishing the base from the noble nor the unjust from the just.

60.4. "To such arrogance, then, has this man—an elder and one who has reaped all the honours from you—filled the folly of the city. Was it worth your while, Valerius, to utter against others reproaches that do not belong to them, when you are yourself liable to such accusations?

61.1. "Against the slanders uttered by this man, what has been said suffices. But concerning the matters about which you have assembled to deliberate, I think it both just and worthy of the city and expedient for you—not only what I declared at the first, but, persisting in the same opinion now too, I declare—not to confound the order of the polity, nor to disturb the unalterable customs of our fathers, nor to abolish from among men faith, a sacred thing, with which every city is safely governed, nor to yield to a people senseless and craving unjust and unlawful deeds.

61.2. "And so far am I from bowing any part of my opinion through fear of those at variance with us—who, banding against me the commons in the city, try to frighten me—that I am far more strongly fixed in my anger than before, and am doubly indignant at the demands of the people; and I have marvelled, senators, at the strangeness of your opinion, that, having not granted it cancellations of debts and release from condemnations when it was not yet plainly an enemy and asked for them, now, when it is in arms and does the deeds of enemies, you deliberate whether you will concede these things—and whatever else may seem good to it; and it will think fit, doubtless, and will make this the first of its demands, to be of equal honour and to share

61.3. the same things with us. Will not affairs, then, come round to a democracy, the most ignorant, as I said, of polities among men, and disadvantageous to you who think fit to rule others? Not if you are wise. Or you would be the most senseless of all, if, having deemed it intolerable to be ruled by one tyrannic man, you now hand yourselves over to a many-headed tyranny, the people, and grant it these things not as it persuades you with favours, but overpowered by necessity and as men yielding against their will, since it is not possible now to do otherwise.

61.4. "But when folly, instead of being punished for its offences, gains honour for them too, how arrogant and haughty, think you, will it be? For do not be lifted up by this hope, that the people will be moderate in its demands, if it become plain to it that you have all so voted.

62.1. "But most of all in this Menenius has been deceived in his judgment—a temperate man, who from his own ways conjectures good of others. For it will press upon you grievously beyond what is fitting, through the arrogance which is wont always to attend on power, and through the folly, of which the multitude shares the greatest part; and if not at the first, at least in time afterward, and at each thing it asks and fails to obtain, it will take up arms and set upon you haughtily in the same way. So that if you concede the first things, thinking them expedient, you will at once be commanded something worse, and again another thing harder than this, since you obeyed the first too through fear, until in the end they cast you from the city—as in many other places, and most recently in Syracuse, the landholders were driven out by their clients.

62.2. "But if you mean to be indignant at those things and oppose their demands, why do you not begin straightway to have free spirits? For it is better, setting out from a lesser cause, before you have been harmed at all, to display your nobility, than, having endured many things, then to be indignant about what has happened and not to entrust the rest, and late to begin to have sense. Let no one of you be frightened either by the agitation of the seceders or by the war of the foreigners; nor condemn your own force as not sufficient to save the city.

62.3. "For the strength of the exiles is small and will not hold out long, remaining, as now, in the open under huts in the wintry season, and unable to provide its necessities—not by plunder, when it has consumed what it has, nor by buying and importing from elsewhere, through poverty, men who have no money either privately or in common; and wars for the most part hold out by surpluses of money; and anarchy, as is likely, and the faction arising from anarchy, falling upon them, will quickly dissolve and break up their counsels.

62.4. "For surely they will not think fit, having surrendered themselves to Sabines or Tyrrhenians or any other foreigners, to be slaves to those whose freedom they themselves once took away along with you; and least of all will they be trusted by them—men who eagerly sought to destroy their own country basely and shamefully—not to do the like to the city that receives them. And all the nations round about you are governed by aristocracy, and in no city does the populace lay claim to equality; so that surely the leading men in each city, who do not allow their own crowd to make disturbance, will not receive this intrusive and factious one into their own country, lest, not having shared like rights themselves, they be in time deprived of equality.

62.5. "But if indeed I err in judgment and some city should receive them, there they will be recognised as enemies and will suffer the lot of enemies. And we have as hostages their fathers and wedded wives and the rest of their kin, than which we could not, even praying, ask better of the gods; whom, setting them in sight of their kinsmen, we will destroy, if they dare to come to grips, as men about to use them with the uttermost outrages. And themselves, if they learn this, know well, you will get supplicating, lamenting, surrendering themselves to us without their arms, enduring everything. For such necessities are dreadful and able to break and cast to nothing all arrogant calculations.

63.1. "These are the reasons why I think the war from the exiles is not to be feared. As for the terrors from the foreigners, it is not now first that they will be tested and found to be such only in word; before too, as often as they gave us trial of themselves, they appeared less than their reputation. And those who think the city's own force not sufficient, and on this account most dread the war, let them learn that they have not adequately perceived it.

63.2. "Against the seceders among the citizens we shall have a counterbalancing force, if we wish, by choosing the most vigorous of our servants and freeing them. For it is better to grant freedom to these than to be deprived of our empire by those; and they have sufficient experience of war, having often been present with us on the campaigns.

63.3. "Against the foreign enemies let us go ourselves with all zeal, and bring all our clients and what is left of the commons. And that this last may be eager for the contests, let us grant it release from debts—not in common, but man by man. For if we must yield to the times and use moderation, let this moderation not be toward our enemy citizens, but toward our friends, to whom we shall seem to give favours not under compulsion but of persuasion. And if there be need of yet other help, this not sufficing, let us summon those from the forts and recall those in the colonies.

63.4. "How great a multitude this is, it would be easy to learn from the most recent census. There are a hundred and thirty thousand Romans of military age registered, of whom the exile element would not be a seventh part. And I do not count the thirty cities of the Latins, which would with much prayer welcome the contests on our behalf, on account of kinship, if you should but vote them equal citizenship, which they continually keep asking for.

64.1. "And that which is the strongest of all in wars, which you yourselves have not yet considered, nor any of the counsellors mentions—this I will add and then cease. There is nothing of which those who would have a fortunate issue of their contests have such need as of good generals. Of these our city is rich, but those of our adversaries are poor.

64.2. "For numerous forces, when they get commanders who do not know how to rule, behave unseemly and are for the most part tripped up by their own size, and suffer the more, the greater toil they have; but good generals, even if they get small forces, quickly make them great. So that, so long as we have men able to lead, we shall not lack those willing to be ruled.

64.3. "Reflecting, then, on these things and remembering the city's deeds, vote nothing humble or ignoble or unworthy of yourselves. What, then, if someone should ask me, do I advise you to do? For perhaps you have long been eager to know this. Neither to send any embassy to the seceders, nor to vote a cancellation of debts, nor to do anything else that might seem a token of fear and helplessness; but if, laying down their arms, they come down to the city and put it in your power to deliberate about them, then, examining at leisure, to use moderation toward them, knowing that all that is senseless—especially if it be a crowd—is wont to grow arrogant toward the humble, but to be humbled toward the arrogant."

65.1. When Claudius had ceased, a great clamour and extraordinary tumult held the council for a long while. For those who seemed aristocratic and thought it right to look to the more just before the unjust attached themselves to the opinion of Claudius and urged the consuls, best of all, to join the stronger party, considering that they held a kingly, not a popular, magisterial power; or, failing that, to keep themselves neutral and let neither faction prevail, and, having counted the opinions of the councillors, to side with the more numerous opinions.

65.2. But if, disregarding both of these, they should make themselves masters of the settlements, they said they would not permit them, but would oppose them with all zeal, with words while they could, and with arms when it became necessary. And this was a strong body, and almost the whole youth of the patricians held to this purpose.

65.3. But those who desired peace attached themselves to the opinion of Menenius and Valerius, and especially the advanced in age, reflecting on the disasters that befall cities from civil wars. Being overborne by the shouting and disorder of the young men, and suspecting their ambition, and fearing the violence they were making against the consuls—that it would come not far short of blows, unless someone yielded to them—they ended by turning to tears and entreaties of their opponents.

66.1. When the tumult had abated and silence came, after a while the consuls, having conferred a little among themselves, brought forth this as the conclusion of their opinion: "We, senators, thought it best of all that all of you should be of one mind, especially in deliberating about the common safety; but, failing that, that the younger should yield to the elder among you and not contend, reflecting that to them too, when they reach this age, it will fall to receive equal honour from their descendants. But since we see you fallen into a most destructive strife—the deadliest of human diseases—and much arrogance attending your young men, for now, since little of the day is left and your resolutions could not reach an end in it, depart from the council; and at the next assembly you will come more moderate and with better opinions.

66.2. "But if your contentiousness remains, we will use the young no longer as judges or counsellors of what is expedient, but for the future will check their disorder by fixing by law the number of years which those who deliberate must have; and giving the word again to the elder, if they agree on nothing in their opinions, we will end their contention by a quick road, which it is better for you to hear and learn beforehand.

66.3. "You know, doubtless, that we have a law, from the time we have dwelt in this city, that the senate is mistress of all things, save to appoint magistrates, to ratify laws, and to declare war or to end one in being; of these three the people has the power by casting its vote. And at present we deliberate about nothing other than war and peace, so that there is much necessity that the people, becoming master of the vote, should ratify our opinions.

66.4. "Having ordered the multitude, therefore, according to this law to come to the Forum, when you have declared your opinions, we will give it the vote, thinking that thus your strife would best be lifted; and whatever the majority votes, this we shall hold valid. Worthy, surely, to obtain this honour are those who remain well-disposed to the city and are to share equally with us in evils and goods."

67.1. Having said this, they dissolved the assembly. On the following days, having ordered that all in the fields and forts should be summoned, and having proclaimed to the senate to come on the same day, when they perceived that the city was full of crowds and that the opinions of the patricians were being overborne by the entreaties which the fathers and infant children of the seceders made with wailing and lamentation, on the appointed day they went out to the Forum, which from much

67.2. of the night was crowded throughout with a multifarious throng. And coming forward to the temple of Vulcan, where it was their custom to hold the assemblies, first they praised the people for the eagerness and zeal of their coming in such numbers; then they urged them to wait quietly until the senate's preliminary decree should be made; and to the kinsmen of the seceders they advised good hopes, as men who would before long recover their dearest. After this, going into the council, they themselves discoursed reasonable and moderate words, and thought fit that the others too should declare kindly and humane opinions. First of all the rest they called Menenius; who, rising, used the same words as before, summoning the senate to the reconciliation, and declared the same opinion, thinking fit to send an embassy to the seceders quickly with full powers for the settlement.

68.1. After him rose, called by age, those who had held the consular office, to all of whom it seemed best to use the opinion of Menenius, until the word came down to Appius. He, rising, said: "I see that it is acceptable both to the consuls, senators, and to almost all the rest of you to bring back the people on whatever terms it itself thinks fit; and I alone of all am left of those who opposed the settlement, remaining hateful to them and no longer of any use to you.

68.2. "Yet not on this account will I depart from what I resolved from the first, nor will I willingly leave my post in the polity. The more deserted I become of those who chose the same things as I, the more honoured I shall be by you at some time hereafter; and praise shall be mine while I live, and, when I am dead, remembrance from those who come after. May it be, then, O Capitoline Jupiter and gods who watch over our city, heroes and divinities, as many as oversee the land of the Romans, that the return of the exiles be fair and expedient for all, and may I be proved false in the hopes

68.3. I hold for the future. But if any evil befall the city from these counsels—and this will be plain before long—may you yourselves give swift correction to it and sure safety to the commonwealth, and to me, who neither on any other occasion chose to say what is pleasant rather than what is most useful, nor now betray the common good while contriving my own private safety,

68.4. be gracious and kind. To the gods, then, I pray these things, for there is no longer need of words; but my opinion, which I declare as before, is that those of the commoners who remain in the city be released from their debts, but that we war with all zeal against the seceders, so long as they remain in arms."

69.1. Having said this, he ceased. When the opinions of the elders had attached themselves to that of Menenius, and the word came down to the younger, the whole senate being upright, there rose Spurius Nautius, successor of one of the most illustrious houses; for the founder of their line, Nautius, was one of those who set out the colony with Aeneas, who was priest of Athena Polias and carried off the image of the goddess when he migrated, which others kept by succession, those of the line of the Nautii; and he was thought, both for his own valour, to be the most brilliant of the young men, and that before long he would attain the consular power.

69.2. Beginning to make a common defence on behalf of all the young men—that they had used neither contentiousness toward their fathers nor arrogance when they held the contrary purpose in the former senate, but, if at all they erred, they erred through their youth in failing of judgment—he ended by saying that he would furnish the proof of this in their change of mind. At all events, he said, they yielded to them as wiser, to vote everything they thought expedient for the commonwealth, since they at least would oppose nothing of these things, but

69.3. would obey their elders. When the other young men declared the like with him, except a very few of Appius' kinsmen, the consuls, praising their good order and exhorting them to show themselves such in all common affairs, chose as envoys the ten most distinguished of the elders, all but one of consular rank. Those appointed were these: Agrippa Menenius Lanatus, son of Gaius; Manius Valerius, son of Volusus...; Publius Servilius, son of Publius...; Publius Postumius Tubertus, son of Quintus; Titus Aebutius Flavius, son of Titus; Servius Sulpicius Camerinus, son of Publius; Aulus Postumius Balbus, son of Publius; Aulus Verginius Caelimontanus, son of Aulus.

69.4. After this, the senate being dissolved, the consuls, coming forward to the assembly, read the decree of the senate and brought forward the envoys; and when all thought fit to learn the instructions given to them, they said in public: to do, in whatever way they could, the making of friendship for the people with the patricians without guile and deceit, and to bring back the fugitives to their own with speed.

70.1. The envoys, having received these instructions from them, set out the same day. Rumour, outrunning their coming, announced to those in the camp all that had happened in the city, and at once all, leaving the stronghold, met the envoys while they were still on the road. There was in the camp a certain very turbulent and factious man, sharp in mind to foresee something of what was to come from afar, and able to say what he thought, being talkative and not without glibness, who was called Lucius Junius, of the same name as the one who overthrew the kings; and, wishing to fulfil the namesake, he thought fit to be surnamed Brutus too. To the many, then, laughter at the man's empty pretension came, and whenever they wished to mock him they called him Brutus.

70.2. This man, having taught Sicinius, the commander of the camp, that it was not better for the people lightly to entrust itself to the proposals, lest, from a lesser claim, it should find its return the more dishonourable, but to hold out for a long while and put a kind of feigned tragedy upon affairs, and having promised that he himself would take up the speech on behalf of the people and having laid down the rest of what should be done or said, persuaded Sicinius. After this Sicinius, summoning the people to an assembly, bade the envoys speak about what they had come for.

71.1. Coming forward, Manius Valerius, who was the eldest and most popular of them, the multitude witnessing his zeal with most kindly cries and salutations, when he had obtained silence, used such words as these: "There is nothing now to hinder you, commoners, from returning again to your own and being reconciled with the fathers.

71.2. "For the senate has voted you a fair and expedient return, and has made it its resolve to bear no rancour for anything that has happened; and us, whom it knew to be most devoted to the people and honoured by you for our justice, it has sent as envoys, having invested us with full powers for the settlement, that, not using opinions and conjectures about your mind, but hearing from yourselves on what terms you think fit to end the dissension—if any of your demands be moderate and hindered neither by impossibility nor by some other irreparable disgrace—we may grant them to you, no longer awaiting the council's opinion, nor putting off matters to long delays and the envy of opponents.

71.3. "The senate having thus voted, receive their favours gladly, commoners, with all eagerness and zeal, accounting it a great thing—such great good fortune—and owing much thanks to the gods for it, if the city of the Romans, ruling so many men, and a council that holds the leadership of all the goods in it, though it is not their ancestral way to yield to any of their adversaries, bow to you alone in their claim willingly, and have neither thought fit to bargain precisely about what befits each party, as superiors with inferiors, but themselves were first to send an embassy about a settlement, nor received with anger your arrogant answers, which you made to the former envoys, but endured this proud and boyish weight of your arrogance, like good fathers with foolish children; and thought fit to send yet another embassy and to take less than their due and to endure everything, citizens, that is

71.4. moderate. Standing, then, on such good fortune, do not delay to say, commoners, what you need, nor trifle with us, but, ending the strife, depart rejoicing to the city that bore and reared you—to which you rendered no fair returns for your nurture, leaving it, as far as in you lay, deserted and a pasture for sheep. But if you let slip this opportunity, you will often pray to find another like it."

72.1. When Valerius had ceased, Sicinius came forward and said that those who deliberate well ought to examine the expedient not from a single argument, but to set before themselves the opposing argument too, especially when considering matters of such moment; and he thought fit that those who wished should speak to these things, laying aside all shame and reserve; for the affairs, shut up in such necessities, permitted them to yield neither to hesitation nor to

72.2. shame. When silence fell—since all looked at one another seeking the one who would speak for the common good, but none appeared, for Sicinius kept using the same words—there came forward, according to his promise, that Lucius Junius, the one who wished to be surnamed Brutus, and, having met with a sudden burst of applause from the multitude, delivered such a harangue:

72.3. "The fear of the patricians, commoners, still frozen in your souls, seems to dismay you, and on this account, being humbled, you hesitate to bring out into the open the words you are accustomed to use among yourselves. And perhaps each of you thinks his neighbour will speak for the common good, and that all rather, if there be any risk, will endure it, while he himself, having stood in safety, will, of whatever good comes from daring, have his share without fear—an ill calculation. For if all of us should suppose this, the cowardice of each one of you singly will become a common harm to all, and in seeking his own private safety each man

72.4. will destroy the common good of all. But if you did not before know that your fear is loosed and that you hold your freedom securely along with your arms, learn it now at least, using these men as teachers. For the haughty and harsh come now not commanding you as before, nor threatening, but begging and exhorting you to return to your own, and they begin to deal with you as with free men on equal terms. Why, then, are you still dismayed at them and silent, and do not have free spirits and, breaking your bridles at last, say in common what you have suffered at their hands? O wretched men,

72.5. what do you fear? That you will suffer some harm by using me as leader of your free speech? For I will risk it on your behalf, speaking what is just with frankness to them, and I will hide nothing. And since Valerius said there was nothing to hinder you from returning to your homes, the senate granting the return and having voted besides to bear no rancour, I will answer him these things, which are true and necessary to be said.

73.1. "There are, Valerius, many other things to hinder us from laying down our arms and putting ourselves in your power, but three the greatest and most manifest. First, that you come accusing us as wrongdoers and think to grant the return as a kind of benefit; next, that you give no hint, in summoning us to the reconciliation, on what just and humane terms we shall make it; and last, that nothing of what you may promise is sure to us, but you have continued often to deceive and cheat us.

73.2. "I will speak of each separately, beginning from the just; for both privately and in public one ought to begin from the just. We, then, if we are wronging you at all, need neither impunity nor amnesty; and indeed we do not even think fit to share in the city any longer, but will endure, wherever necessity may lead us, entrusting ourselves to fortune and the divinities as guides. But if, being wronged by you, we have been forced to make trial of the fortune in which we are, why do you not confess that you yourselves, having dealt ill with us, need pardon and amnesty? But now you say you grant what you ask for, and the anger from which you seek to be freed, this you boast as though you were remitting it—confounding the nature of truth and reversing the claim of justice.

73.3. "That you are not wronged but do the wrong, and, having received many great benefits from the people—some toward freedom, some toward empire—have rendered it no fair returns, learn. And I will make my arguments from facts which you yourselves know; and, by the gods, if I say anything false, do not endure it, but at once refute me.

74.1. "Our ancient polity was monarchy, and we continued to use this polity down to the seventh generation; and through all these leaderships the people was never at any time worsted by the kings, and least of all by the last; I forbear to say that it reaped many great goods from their rule.

74.2. "For, apart from the rest of their courting of it—by which, flattering it, they wished it to be their own and your enemy, which all do who manage their power in tyrannic fashion—when they had conquered after a long war Suessa, a most prosperous city, though they might have shared the spoils with no one but kept them themselves and surpassed all kings in wealth, they did not think fit to do so, but brought all the booty into the common stock; so that we, apart from slaves and cattle and the rest of the possessions, which were many and fair, distributed five minae of silver per man.

74.3. "Neglecting these things, when they used their power more tyrannically—erring not against the people but against you—we, ill-bearing what was being done, withdrew from goodwill toward the kings and attached ourselves to you; and rising up against them with you, both those in the city and those in the camp, we expelled them and, bringing it to you, entrusted to you their power. And though it was often in our power to go over to the exiles for the great gifts they held out to us, that we might abandon our faith to you, we did not endure it, but drained off many great and continuous wars and dangers on your behalf; and to the present, this seventeenth year now, we have been worn out fighting all men for the common freedom.

74.4. "For while the polity was still unsettled—as is wont to happen amid changes made suddenly—against two of the most distinguished cities of the Tyrrhenians, the Tarquinienses and the Veientes, who wished to bring back the kings with a great army, we, few against many, ventured and fought it out, and, displaying the greatest zeal, conquered in battle and drove off those arrayed against us, and with the surviving consul preserved the magistracy.

74.5. "Not long after, when Porsina, king of the Tyrrhenians, himself thought fit to bring back the exiles, with the force from all Tyrrhenia which he led and those long since gathered by the exiles, we, having no force a match for them and on this account shut up in a siege and helplessness and want of every resource, by enduring all the terrors compelled him, become our friend, to depart.

74.6. "Last of all, when the kings had prepared a third return through the Latin nation and were bringing thirty cities against us, seeing you supplicating and lamenting and each one of you calling upon us, reminding us of comradeship and fellowship of rearing and brotherhood in arms, we did not endure to abandon you; but, thinking it the fairest and most brilliant contest, the one on your behalf, we advanced against the perils, hazarding that greatest of dangers, in which, receiving many wounds and losing many persons of kinsmen and comrades and tent-mates, we conquered the enemy and slew their commanders and destroyed the whole royal kindred.

75.1. "These are the things we furnished beyond our strength, through our own eagerness, toward freeing you from the tyrants, set to it not by necessity more than by valour. Now hear what we did toward your being honoured and ruling others and putting on a dominion greater than the original expectation; and, if I turn the speech aside at all from the truth, as I said at the beginning, oppose

75.2. me. For you, when the safety of your freedom seemed secure, did not think it enough to remain at this, but, rushing to daring and innovation—and perhaps thinking all that surrounds freedom an enemy, and well-nigh proclaiming war against all men—you thought fit to use our bodies for all the ventures and contests on behalf of this greed.

75.3. "How many cities, then, waging war against you one and two at a time for their freedom, we made subject—some overcoming them in pitched battle, some taking them by storm of their walls—I pass over. For why should I tell the deeds bit by bit, having such abundance of arguments? But all Tyrrhenia, divided into twelve principalities and abounding in power great both by land and by sea—who were they that helped win it and made it subject to you? And these Sabines here, a nation so great, with whom you had ever the contest for the primacy—what aid afforded you no longer to dispute over equality? And what of the thirty cities of the Latins, lifted up not only by greatness of power but also proud in claiming the more just—who were they that enslaved them and made them, begging against the enslavement and razing of their cities, flee for refuge to you?

76.1. "I pass over the rest—how, while not yet at variance with you, and ourselves laying claim to the hopes from empire, we shared the dangers with you. But when you had plainly clothed your magistracy in tyranny and were proved to be treating us like slaves, and we no longer remained the same in our minds toward you, and at the same time nearly all the subjects were rising in revolt—the Volscians beginning the rebellion, and following them the Aequians, Hernicans, Sabines, and many others—and it seemed there was such an opportunity as no other, had we wished it, to accomplish one of two things, either to overthrow your empire or to render it more moderate for the future—do you remember into what despair of empire you came and how you were utterly dispirited, whether we should not join the contests with you or, in anger, turn against you as enemies, and how many entreaties and promises you made?

76.2. "What, then, did we, the humble and insulted by you, do then? Worsted by your entreaties and persuaded by the promises which this excellent Servilius, then consul, made to the people, we bore no rancour for the old wrongs, but, hoping for good things for the time to come, gave ourselves to you, and, having in a short time finished all the warlike work, came back leading many prisoners and fair booty.

76.3. "In return for which, what thanks did you render us? Just thanks, worthy of the dangers? Whence? Far from it. You falsified the promises which you bade the consul make on behalf of the commonwealth, and the man himself, this excellent one whom you used for the deceit, you made to have no share in the triumph, though most of all men deserving to obtain this honour, fixing on him the insult for no other reason than that he thought fit you should do what is just as you had promised, and was plainly indignant at the deceit.

77.1. "And lately—for, adding this to my speech about the just, I will cease—when the Aequians and Sabines and Volscians, using one mind, both themselves rose up and summoned the rest, were you not forced to flee for refuge to us, the humble and base, you the grave and weighty, promising everything for your safety then? And, that you might not seem to deceive us again, which you often did, you found as a veil for the deceit this Manius Valerius, the most popular of men; trusting in whom, that we should not be deceived by a dictator, and that a man kind toward us, we joined you in this war too and conquered the enemy, enduring contests not small nor few nor obscure.

77.2. "But when the fairest part of the war had reached its end sooner than the hope of all, so far were you from rejoicing and owing much thanks to the people, that you thought fit to keep us still, against our will, under the standards in arms, that you might evade the promises as you had resolved from the first. And when the man would not endure the deceit nor the shame of the deed, but brought the standards into the city and dismissed the forces to their homes, making this a pretext for not doing what was just, you insulted him, and observed none of your agreements with us, but in the same act committed three of the greatest crimes: abolishing the dignity of the senate, destroying the faith of the man, and making unprofitable to your benefactors the thanks for their toils.

77.3. "Having these and many other like things to say to you, patricians, we do not think fit to turn to supplications and entreaties of you, nor, like those who have done dreadful deeds, to receive our return on impunity and amnesty. Yet we do not think we ought to argue precisely about these things at present, since we have assembled to discourse about concord, but we let them go, consigning them to neglect and oblivion.

78.1. "But on what terms you make your embassy, and what you have come to ask, why do you not say plainly? On what hopes do you think fit that we return to the city? Having taken what fortune as guide of the road? With what cheer or joy to receive us? For up to now we hear you holding forth nothing humane or good—no honours, no offices, no remedy for poverty, nothing whatever at all. And yet you ought not to say what you are about to do, but, having done it, to say it, that, having already received some deed done from goodwill, we might conjecture the rest

78.2. will be such. I suppose, then, they will say to this that they have come with full powers, so that whatever we persuade one another of shall be valid. Let this be true; let what follows from it come to pass; I make no objection. But I wish to learn from them what will be after this—when we have said on what terms we think fit to make the return, and these have been conceded by them—who will be the guarantor to us of the agreements?

78.3. "Trusting what security shall we lay our arms from our hands and put our persons again into their power? The decrees of the senate to be written about these things—for not yet written? And what again will prevent these from being annulled by other decrees, whenever it seems good to Appius and those who think like him? Or the dignity of the envoys, who pledge their own faith? But it was through these very men that they deceived us before. Or, having procured pledges from them by oaths in covenants before the gods? But I, beyond all human faith, fear this—which I see despised by those in power; and the involuntary compacts of those who claim to rule toward those who lay claim to freedom, not now first but having often learned of, I know hold good only so long as their necessities prevail.

78.4. "What, then, is such a friendship and faith, in which we shall be forced to court one another against our judgment, each side watching its own opportunities? And after this, suspicions and continual slanders against one another, envies and hatreds and every other form of evils, and a great contest as to who shall first destroy his rival, suffering lying in the future delay.

79.1. "And of a civil war, as all know, there is nothing worse, in which the conquered are unfortunate and the conquerors do wrong, and it falls to the one to be destroyed by their dearest, to the other to destroy their dearest. To such fortunes and disasters, not to be prayed for, neither do you, patricians, call us, nor let us, commoners, hearken to them; but, as fortune has divided us from one another, let us be content. Let these, then, have the whole city and reap it without us and enjoy all the other goods alone, having cast the humble and inglorious commoners from their country; and let us depart, wherever the divinity may lead us, reckoning that we leave a foreign place, not our own city.

79.2. "For to none of us is there left here a lot of land, nor an ancestral hearth, nor common sacred rites, nor a dignity as in a country, clinging to which we should love the place and remain even against our will; nor even the freedom of our persons won with arms by many toils; since some things the many wars destroyed, others the want of daily necessaries consumed, and others we were robbed of by these arrogant creditors—to whom in the end we wretches were forced to till our own lots, digging, planting, ploughing, tending flocks, fellow slaves to our own war-captured bondsmen, some bound with chains, some with fetters, some, like the fiercest of beasts, with collars and irons.

79.3. "Outrages and insults and lashes and toils from night to night, and every other cruelty and insolence and arrogance which we endured, I pass over. Freed, then, by the divinity from so great and so many evils, let us flee from them gladly, with all the zeal and power each man has, making fortune and god, who save us, our guides on the road, reckoning freedom our country and valour our wealth. For every land will receive us as partners—to those who receive us we shall be, on the one hand, not grievous, on the other, useful.

80.1. "Let there be for us examples of these things many Greeks and many barbarians, but most of all the forefathers of these men and of us; of whom some, rising up with Aeneas from Asia into Europe, founded a city in the land of the Latins, and others, later setting out from Alba under Romulus' leadership of the colony, established in these places the city we now leave.

80.2. "And we have a force not only not a little greater than theirs, but threefold, and a juster cause for the migration. For those who migrated from Ilium were driven out by enemies, but we from here by friends; and surely it is more piteous to be driven out by one's own than by strangers. And those who joined with Romulus
