80.3. in the expedition, for the sake of getting better land, despised their fathers'; but we, leaving the city-less and hearth-less life, set out a colony neither envied by gods nor grievous to men nor a burden to any land; and we have not even come through blood and kindred slaughters against those who drive us out, nor harmed with fire and steel the land we leave, nor left behind any memorial of eternal enmity, as it is the custom for treacherous exiles and those shut up in unwilling necessities

80.4. to do. Calling the gods and divinities to witness, who lead all mortal things according to justice, and leaving to them to exact the penalties on our behalf, we ask only this: that those of us who have in the city infant children and parents and any wives who may wish to share our fortune, take back their persons. This is enough for us to receive, and we need nothing else from our country. But fare you well and live the life you choose, thinking thus in matters of polity and partnership against the humbler sort, alien and unsharing."

81.1. Brutus, then, having spoken such words, ceased; and to those present, all that he said about the just seemed true, and all his accusations of the council's haughtiness, but most of all those in which he showed the security of the agreements full of guile and deceit. When at the end he went through the outrages they had suffered from the creditors, and reminded each man of his own evils, no one was so hard in mind that he did not melt into tears and bewail the common misfortunes; and this happened not to them alone, but also to those come from the senate. For not even the envoys had strength to restrain their tears, reflecting on the calamities arising from the dividing of the city; and there was a long time in which, downcast and tearful and at a loss

81.2. what to say, they stood. When the great lamentation had ceased and silence held the assembly, there came forward to make defence against these things one who seemed to surpass the other citizens in age and dignity, Titus Larcius, who, twice appointed consul, having used the power called dictatorship best of all men, made that envied office be reckoned holy and full of reverence.

81.3. Setting out to make speeches about the just—blaming the creditors as having done cruel and inhuman deeds, but laying hold of the poor as not justly thinking fit to be released from their debts by force rather than by favour, and as not rightly being angry with the senate because they obtained none of the moderate things from it,

81.4. rather than with the guilty; and trying to show that small was the part of the people that did wrong unwillingly, forced by the length of its poverty to ask for the release, but the greater part, given over to licence and insolence and living by pleasures and prepared to serve its desires by plunder from others' goods; and thinking that the wretched must be distinguished from the wicked, and those needing humanity from those deserving hatred; and setting up certain other such arguments, true indeed, but not pleasing to all his hearers—he did not persuade, but there was much murmuring at each point, and from some indignation as if he were embittering their griefs, from others acknowledgments as if he hid nothing of the truth; but this latter part was far less than the other, so that they were obliterated by the many, and the cry of the indignant prevailed.

82.1. When Larcius had added a few words more to these and laid hold of their uprising and the rashness of their counsels, Sicinius, who was then leader of the people, taking up the speech, exasperated their tempers still more, saying that from these very words they could best learn what honours and favours would receive them when they returned to their country.

82.2. "For to men who, being at the height of their dangers and needing the people's help and come for this, it does not even now occur to make moderate and humane speeches—what disposition must we think they will assume, when affairs go for them according to their hope, and the things now insulted in words become subject in deeds? From what arrogance will they refrain, from what maltreatment, from what tyrannic cruelty?

82.3. "But if it suffices you to be slaves all the time of your life, bound and scourged and destroyed by fire and steel and famine and every outrage, do not waste time, but, throwing away your arms and putting your two hands behind you, follow them; but if there is in you any longing for freedom, do not endure them. And you, envoys, either say on what just terms you summon us, or, not saying them, depart from the assembly; for we will give you the floor no longer."

83.1. When he ceased, all present applauded as men agreeing with one who had reasoned what was needful; and after this, silence coming, Menenius Agrippa—who had both made the speeches in the senate on behalf of the people and was most responsible for the opinion that the embassy with full powers be sent—signalled that he too wished to speak. To them the matter seemed answered to their prayer, and now at least they supposed they would hear words holding true settlements and saving opinions for both sides.

83.2. And at first all roared out with a great cry, bidding him speak; then they checked themselves, and so great a silence held the assembly that the place differed not at all from a desert. He, in other respects, was thought to have used the most persuasive words possible and aimed at the wish of his hearers; and at the end of his harangue he is said to have told a fable in the manner of Aesop, fashioned to have much likeness to the affairs, and by this most of all to have won them—whence the speech is deemed worthy of remembrance and is borne in all the ancient histories. What was said by him was as follows:

83.3. "We were sent by the senate to you, commoners, neither to make defence on its behalf nor to accuse you; for these things did not seem to have their season nor to be suited to the fortunes that grip the commonwealth; but to dissolve the strife with all zeal and contrivance and to set the polity back into its original order, having the full power for this. So that concerning the just we do not think there is need, as Junius here did, to spin out the time at great length; but on what humane terms we think the strife should be dissolved, and what faith there will be to confirm our agreements—about these things,

83.4. which we have resolved, we will speak to you. To us, reflecting that every strife is healed in every city when the causes that furnished the difference are removed, it seemed necessary to recognise and stop the very pretexts that began the dissension. Finding that the harsh exactions of the loans had become the causes of the present evils, thus we correct them: we think it just that all who owe debts and cannot discharge them be released from their obligations; and if the persons of any who are past due are held by the lawful terms, these too we judge to be free; and as many as, convicted in private suits, have been handed over to those who condemned them, these too we wish to be free, and we make void their condemnations.

83.5. "Concerning the contracts of past time, then, which we judge made the secession, we set them right in this way; concerning those that shall be later, as shall seem good to you, the people, and to those of the council deliberating in common, a law being ratified, so let it stand. Was it not these things that set you apart from the patricians, commoners, and, if you obtained them, did you think they sufficed you and you reached for nothing else? They are now given you; depart at once rejoicing to your country.

84.1. "The pledges that will confirm these agreements and furnish you security shall be all such as are lawful and customary among those who dissolve enmities. The senate will vote these things and give the rank of law to what shall be written; or rather, let what is resolved be written here by you, and the senate will obey it.

84.2. "That the things now conceded shall remain firm, and that nothing contrary to them shall later be brought forward by the senate—first we, the envoys, are sureties, giving you our persons and souls and offspring as pledges; next the other senators, as many as shall be enrolled with the decree; for surely nothing will ever be written against the people without our consent. For we who lead the council and first declare our opinions of the rest are we.

84.3. "The last pledge for all men, Greeks and barbarians, which no time will ever abolish, is that which, by oaths and covenants, makes the gods sureties of the agreements; by which many bitter enmities of private men, and many wars set up between cities, have been reconciled. And if you take this pledge, either entrust to a few of the leaders of the council to give you the oaths on behalf of the whole senate, or think fit that all who are enrolled in the decrees swear over sacrifices that they will in very truth keep firm the things agreed.

84.4. "Right hands and covenants and pledges made before the gods do not you slander, Brutus, nor abolish the fairest of human practices; nor do you, commoners, endure him saying that they are the knaveries of unholy and tyrannic men, which are far from the valour of the Romans.

85.1. "Having spoken of one more pledge, which is neither unknown to any man nor disputed, I will cease. And what is this? That which introduces the common interest and makes both parts be saved through one another. This, indeed, first and alone draws us together to the same place and will never let us be apart from one another. For the ignorant multitude will always need, and will never cease needing, intelligent leadership, and the council able to lead will need the crowds willing to be ruled; and not by opinion alone

85.2. have we conjectured this, but by deed have we made trial and know it. Why, then, do we frighten and make trouble for one another? Why do we speak base words, when we have good deeds in hand, instead of, opening ourselves and throwing our two arms about one another, going to our country to recover the old delight of the sweetest things and the longing dearest of all, but seek instead non-existent securities and faithless faiths, like the bitterest enemies who suspect everything for the worse? For us, commoners, of the council, one pledge suffices about your never being base toward us, should you return—we who know your good services in rearing us and your lawful practices and the rest of the valour you have often displayed in peace and in war.

85.3. "And if, through necessity of faith and hope, the contracts should get a common correction, the rest at least we trust will be good on your side, and we need neither oaths nor hostages nor any other pledge whatever from the multitude; we, on the contrary, will oppose nothing of your demands. And concerning the faith, with which Brutus tried to slander us, these things suffice. But if any envy, not just, lurks in you, persuading you to think evil concerning the senate, I wish to speak a word against this too, commoners; and—by the gods—hear me in quiet and with attention.
86.1. "A city is somehow like a human body. For each is compounded and made of many parts; and neither part has the same power as the parts within them, nor furnishes equal services.

86.2. "If, then, the parts of the human body should take each a separate sense and voice of their own, and then strife should fall among them, all the rest becoming of one mind against the belly alone, and the feet should say that the whole body rests upon them; the hands, that they work the crafts and procure the necessaries and fight enemies and furnish many other benefits to the common good; the shoulders, that all the burdens are carried upon them; the mouth, that it speaks; the head, that it sees and hears and, embracing all the other senses, holds them, through which the creature is preserved; and then they should say to the belly: 'But you, good lady, what of these do you do, or what is your favour and benefit to us? Nay, you are so far from doing and helping us accomplish anything of common use, that you even work against us and trouble us, and—a thing unbearable—compel us to serve you and to fetch from every quarter for the filling of your own desires.

86.3. "'Come, why do we not lay claim to freedom and rid ourselves of the many businesses we endure for her sake?' If, then, these things should seem good to them, and each should no longer do its own work, can the body in any way endure for long, but would it not within a few days be consumed by the worst of deaths, famine? One could not say otherwise.

86.4. "In the same way conceive also concerning a city. For many are the peoples that fill it too, in nothing like one another, of whom each furnishes the common good its own particular service, as the limbs do the body. For some till the fields, some fight for them against enemies, some bring in many benefits by sea through trade, others work the necessary crafts. If, then, all these peoples should rise in strife against the council gathered from the best, and say: 'But you, council, what good do you do us, and for what cause do you think fit to rule the others? For you could say nothing.' And then: 'Shall we not rid ourselves of this tyranny of yours at last and dwell without

86.5. "'a leader?' If, then, conceiving these things, they should stand off from their accustomed practices, what will prevent this city from perishing miserably and miserably by famine and war and every other evil? Learning, then, commoners, that just as in our bodies the belly, ill-reviled by the many, nourishes the body while it is nourished and preserves it while it is preserved, and is a kind of common feast distributing to all what is fitting and the cause of the harmony, so in cities the council, which administers the common affairs and provides for what befits each, preserves and guards and sets right everything—cease your envious cries against it, that you were cast from your country and that as wanderers and beggars you go about because of it. For it has done you no harm, nor would it do; but itself it calls and beseeches and, opening its soul along with the gates, receives you."

87.1. While Menenius was saying such things, many and various cries arose from those present throughout the whole harangue. But when at the end of his speech he turned to lamentations and bewailed the misfortunes about to seize both those remaining in the city and those driven out, and the fortunes of both, tears poured from all, and with one accord and one cry they shouted to lead them to the city and not waste time; and very nearly did they hasten to depart from the assembly, having entrusted all affairs to the envoys and contrived nothing further for their security, had not Brutus come forward and checked their impulses, saying that all the rest was well for the people, all that the senate promised, and that they owed it much thanks for the concessions; but that he feared for all time, and lest tyrannic men, attempting it perhaps at some later day,

87.2. should bear rancour against the people for what had happened. There was one only safeguard for all who fear their superiors—if it became plain to them that those who wished to wrong them had no power; but while the ability to do wicked deeds was present, the wicked would not lack the will. If, then, they should obtain this security, they would need nothing further.

87.3. When Menenius interposed and bade him say what security he thought the people still needed, "Grant us," he said, "to appoint magistrates each year from ourselves, however many, who shall have authority over nothing else, but shall help those of the commoners who are wronged or overpowered, and shall not look on while any one is robbed of his rights. This we beseech and beg of you, besides the other things you have granted—if the reconciliation is not word but deed—to give and bestow."

88.1. The people, when they heard this, with a great cry that held a long while both praised the man and urged the envoys to grant them this also. The envoys, withdrawing from the assembly and conferring a little among themselves, returned not long after. When silence fell, Menenius came forward and said: "The matter, commoners, is great and full of many strange suspicions; and fear and concern enter us, lest at some time we make two cities in one; yet, for the part that lies with us, not even against this request of yours do we set ourselves.

88.2. "Only grant us this, which is for your sakes too: allow some of the envoys to go into the city and declare this to the senate; for though we have the power from it to make the settlement however we wish, being autocrats of the promises, we do not think fit ourselves to take this, but, since a new matter has met us beyond expectation, having taken away our own power, we will carry it and lay it upon the council; though we are persuaded that it too will think the same as we. I, then, will remain here and with me a part of the embassy, but Valerius will go and the rest with

88.3. him." These things seemed good; and in haste, mounting their horses, those who were to declare to the senate what had happened rode to the city. When the consuls set the matter before the councillors, the opinion of Valerius was to grant this favour too to the people; but Appius, who from the first had opposed the reconciliation, then too openly spoke against it, shouting and calling the gods to witness and foretelling to the polity how great a seed of evils it was about to sow. But he did not persuade the many, who had set out, as I said, to dissolve the strife. There came, then, a decree of the senate, that all the other things which the envoys had promised the people should be valid, and that the security

88.4. which it asked be granted. The envoys, having arranged these matters, on the following day came to the camp and made clear what the senate had resolved. After this, Menenius advising the commoners to send some to the city, to whom the senate would give the pledges, there was sent Lucius Junius Brutus, of whom I spoke before, and with him Marcus Decius and Spurius Icilius. Of those come from the senate, half returned to the city with Brutus and his colleagues, while Agrippa, with the rest, remained at the camp, being asked to draw up the law for the commoners according to which they would appoint the magistrates.

89.1. On the following day Brutus and his colleagues were present, having made the compacts with the senate through the fetial priests, whom the Romans call Fetiales. The people, divided into the phratries then existing—or however one wishes to call them, which those men call curiae—appoint these annual magistrates: Lucius Junius Brutus and Gaius Sicinius Bellutus, whom they had already as leaders, and besides these Gaius and Publius Licinius and Gaius Visellius Ruga.

89.2. These five men were the first to take up the tribunician power, on the fourth day before the Ides of December, as is done even to our own time. When the elections were completed, to those come from the senate everything seemed well concerning the matters for which they were sent; but Brutus, calling an assembly, advised the commoners to declare the office sacred and inviolable, confirming its security by law and

89.3. oath. These things seemed good to all, and this law was written by him and his colleagues: "Let no one compel a tribune, against his will, to do anything, as if he were one of the many, nor scourge him, nor order another to scourge, nor kill him, nor bid kill. And if anyone do any of the forbidden things, let him be accursed, and let his goods be consecrated to Demeter, and let him who kills any of those who have done these things be

89.4. clear of bloodshed. And, that for the future the people may not have the power to abolish this law, but that it remain unalterable for all time, it was ordained that all Romans swear over sacrifices that they would use the law, both they and their descendants for all time; and a curse was added to the oath, that to those who kept it the heavenly gods and the divinities below be gracious, but to those who transgressed it the opposite both from gods and from divinities, as upon men liable to the greatest guilt. From this it became a custom among the Romans that the persons of the tribunes be sacred and inviolate, and it remains so to our own time."

90.1. When they had voted these things, they built an altar on the height where they had encamped, which from the fear that then held them they named, as their ancestral tongue signifies, of Jupiter Deimatius (the Affrighter); and having performed sacrifices to it and consecrated the place that received them, they came down to the city with the envoys.

90.2. Having rendered thank-offerings also to the gods in the city, and persuaded the patricians to ratify the office by casting their vote, when they had obtained this too from them, they further asked the senate to permit them to appoint each year two men from the commoners who should serve the tribunes in whatever they needed, and should judge the cases which those committed to them, and should take care of the sacred and public places and of the abundance in the market.

90.3. Having received this concession too from the senate, they appoint men whom they called assistants of the tribunes, colleagues, and judges. Now, however, in the native tongue, from one of the works they perform, they are called overseers of sacred places (aediles), and they no longer have a power subservient to others, as before, but many great things have been entrusted to them, and in most respects they somewhat resemble the agoranomoi among the Greeks.

91.1. When affairs had settled and the city recovered its original order, an army was levied by the commanders against the foreign enemies, the people bringing much zeal and in a short time making ready everything needful for the war. When the consuls had cast lots concerning the command, as is their custom, Spurius Cassius, who obtained the care of affairs in the city, remained, taking a sufficient part of the levied force; while Postumus Cominius led out the rest of the army, leading a worthy portion of the Romans themselves and a not small Latin allied force.

91.2. Resolving to attack the Volscians first, he seized at the first assault their city Longula, the men in it having attempted to lay claim to some valour and sent out a force into the open by which they trusted to ward off the assailants, but having been shamefully compelled to flee before displaying any brilliant deed, and having done nothing noble even in the assault on the walls. In a single day, at all events, the Romans both mastered their land without effort and took the city by storm with little trouble.

91.3. The Roman general, allowing the soldiers to plunder the goods found there and leaving a garrison in the city, led the force against another city of the Volscians, called Polusca, which is not far distant from Longula. No one daring to meet him, having traversed the country with much ease, he assaulted the walls; and of the soldiers, some breaking through the gates, others mounting the wall by ladders, on the same day they become masters of this city too.

91.4. When he had taken the city, choosing out a few, the authors of the revolt, he put them to death, and punishing the rest by confiscation of money and depriving them of their arms, he compelled them for the future to be subjects of the Romans.

92.1. Leaving in this city too a small part of the army for a guard, on the following day, taking up the force, he advanced against Corioli, a very notable city and, as it were, the metropolis of the Volscians; where there was a strong force gathered, and the wall was not easy to take, and the necessaries for war had long since been prepared by those within. Attempting the assault on the walls, until late evening he was beaten off by his opponents, losing many of his own men.

92.2. On the next day, having prepared rams and wicker shields and ladders, he was making ready as if to make trial of the city with his whole force; but hearing that the Antiates were about to come to the aid of the Coriolani in great strength, on account of kinship, and that those sent were already on the road, he divided his army, resolving with the half to assault the walls, leaving Titus Larcius in charge of it,

92.3. and with the rest he purposed to bar the assailants. And there were two contests on the same day; and the Romans conquered—all fighting eagerly, but one man displaying incredible valour and performing deeds beyond all telling, who was of the patrician class and of not undistinguished fathers, called Gaius Marcius, a man temperate in his daily life and full of a free spirit. The manner of each of the two battles was as follows. Larcius, leading out the army at daybreak, brought it up to the walls of Corioli and made assaults at many points; but the Coriolani, priding themselves on the help from the Antiates, which they trusted would be present not long after, opening all the gates, rushed in a mass upon the enemy.

92.4. The Romans received their first onset and dealt many blows to those who came to grips; then, as more came on, being thrust down a sloping place, they gave way. Seeing this, Marcius, of whom I spoke before, took his stand with a few and received the oncoming throng of the enemy; and having struck down many of them, when the rest gave way and fled toward the city, he followed, ever killing those at hand and urging the fugitives among his own to turn back and take heart and follow him.

92.5. They, ashamed at the deed, turned again and pressed upon those opposite them, striking and pursuing; and in a short time, each routing those they grappled with, they pressed upon the walls; and Marcius, now daring the danger more boldly, went still further forward, and, coming to the very gates, fell in with the fugitives into the wall. When many others had rushed in with him, in many parts of the city there was much slaughter on both sides—some fighting along the streets, others about the houses being captured.

92.6. The women too within helped the work, hurling tiles from the roofs upon the enemy, and, so far as each had strength and power, eagerly aided their country. Yet they did not hold out long against the perils, but were forced to surrender themselves to the conquerors. The city being thus taken, the rest of the Romans turned to plundering what was found there and continued a long while busy with the spoils, since there was much money in the place and many slaves;

93.1. but Marcius, who first and before many had withstood the enemy and proved the most brilliant of all the Romans both in the assault on the walls and in the contests within them, appeared still more brilliant in the second contest set against the Antiates. For he did not think fit to be absent from this battle either, but, as soon as the city was taken, taking with him the few who could follow, he went at a run, and finding the forces already drawn up and about to come to grips, first announced to his own the capture of the city, showing as its proof the smoke which was being borne up in quantity from the burning houses, and begging the consul, he posted himself against the strongest part of the enemy.

93.2. And when the signals for battle were raised, he was the first to come to grips with the opponents, and, having killed many of those who engaged him, thrust himself into the middle of their phalanx. The Antiates no longer endured to fight him at close quarters, but left their ranks wherever he came on, and, surrounding him in a body, hurled at him as he advanced and pursued, retreating. Postumus, when he learned this, fearing lest the man, being isolated, should suffer some harm, sent the best of the young men to aid him; and they, forming their companies dense, charged the enemy. As those in front did not receive them but turned to flight, advancing further they found Marcius full of wounds and saw about him many corpses lying and men half-dead.

93.3. After this they now advanced in common, with Marcius as leader, against those still remaining in formation, killing those who withstood and treating them like slaves. Worthy of mention, indeed, were the other Romans too in this battle, but the best of them were those who had shielded Marcius; and above all Marcius himself, who was unquestionably the chief author of the victory. When it was now growing dark, the Romans withdrew to their camp, thinking highly of the victory and having both killed many of the Antiates and leading many prisoners.

94.1. On the following day Postumus, summoning the army to an assembly, went through much praise of Marcius and bound him with crowns of valour, rendering thank-offerings for both contests. He presented him with a war-horse adorned with the trappings of a general and ten captive persons, leaving it to him to take whom he wished, and as much silver as he himself could carry away, and from the rest of the booty many fair first-fruits.

94.2. When a great cry arose from all, as men praising and rejoicing with him, Marcius, coming forward, said he owed great thanks both to the consul and to all the rest for the honours with which they deemed him worthy; yet he would not avail himself of them, but would be content with the horse, for the splendour of its trappings, and one captive, who happened to be his guest-friend. The soldiers, who before too had admired the man for his nobility, marvelled still more at his disdain of wealth and that he bore so great good fortune with moderation. From this deed he was surnamed Coriolanus, and had become the most distinguished of all those of his age.

94.3. When the battle against the Antiates had reached this end, the rest of the cities of the Volscians dissolved their enmity toward the Romans; and as many as held the like sentiments with them—those already in arms and those preparing for war—ceased. Dealing with all these with moderation, Postumus returned home and disbanded the army. Cassius, the other of the consuls, who had been left in Rome, dedicated in the meantime the temple of Demeter and Dionysus and Cora, which is set up at the boundaries of the largest of the circuses, above the very starting-stalls—Aulus Postumius the dictator having vowed on behalf of the city to dedicate it to the gods, at the time when he was about to contend against the Latin army, and the senate after the victory having voted that its entire building be made from the spoils; and it then received its completion.

24.1. At the same time new treaties also were made, with oaths, with all the cities of the Latins for peace and friendship, since they had attempted no disturbance in the strife and were plainly rejoicing in the return of the people, and seemed ready to share in the war against the seceders.

24.2. What was written in the treaties was as follows: "Let there be peace between the Romans and all the cities of the Latins toward one another, so long as heaven and earth keep the same station; and let them neither make war on one another, nor bring in wars from elsewhere, nor furnish safe roads to those who bring war; and let them help with all their power those who are warred upon; and of the spoils and booty from common wars let each side obtain an equal share; and let the judgments of private contracts be made within ten days, in whatever place the contract was made. To these treaties let it be permitted neither to add anything nor to take anything from them, save what shall seem good to the Romans and all the Latins."

24.3. These things, then, the Romans and the Latins agreed with one another, swearing over sacrifices. And the senate voted also to render thank-offerings to the gods for the reconciliation with the people, adding one day to the so-called Latin Festivals, which were two: the first having been consecrated by King Tarquinius, at the time when he conquered the Tyrrhenians; the other added by the people, when, having expelled the kings, it made the city free; to which the third was then assigned for the sake of the return of the seceders.

24.4. The presidency and the care of the sacrifices and games held in them the assistants of the tribunes took over—those who now have the aedilician power, as I said—adorned by the senate with purple and an ivory chair and the other insignia which the kings had.

96.1. Not long after the festival, one of the consulars, Menenius Agrippa, ended his life—he who had conquered the Sabines and led home a most brilliant triumph over them, by whom the senate, being persuaded, granted the return to the exiles, and the people, trusting him, laid down their arms; and the city buried him at public charge and with the fairest and most splendid funeral of all men. For the man had no estate sufficient for the magnificence of a funeral procession and burial; so that even to the guardians of his children, when they deliberated, it seemed best to bring him out and bury him cheaply, as one of the many.

96.2. But the people did not allow it; rather, the tribunes, gathering the multitude into an assembly and going through many encomiums of the man's deeds both in war and in civic affairs, and his temperance and the frugality of his life, but most of all extolling with their praises to the utmost his self-restraint with regard to money-making, said it was the most shameful of things that so great a man should obtain an obscure and humble burial through poverty; and they exhorted the people to undertake the expense and to contribute man by man as much as they themselves should

96.3. appoint. To the hearers it was welcome, and at once, each bringing what was appointed, a great sum of money was gathered. The senate, learning this, took the matter as a disgrace and resolved not to look on while the most distinguished of the Romans was buried by a man-by-man collection, but judged that the expense should be made from the public funds, entrusting the care to the quaestors. They, contracting for the provisions at very much money and adorning his body with the most costly array and supplying everything else for magnificence, buried him worthily of his valour.

96.4. And the people, vying with the senate in honour, did not even think fit to take back the sum contributed, though the quaestors returned it, but bestowed it on the man's children, pitying their poverty, that they might do nothing unworthy of their father's valour. There was also a census at this time through the consuls, from which were found more than a hundred and ten thousand persons in all who registered. And these were the things done by the Romans in the consulship of these men.
